passage:
Dear Jasleen,

I keep replaying the wedding. When I said I disagreed with the government on one policy, a distant relative called me brainwashed and anti-national, loudly, with people listening. My cheeks burned. I wanted to fire back with everything I had.

Instead I said, "I see it differently, and I care about this country as much as you do. I'm going to get some tea." And I went. That was all. Nobody won.

I've been asking myself why it hurt so much. I think it's being turned into a label, when I'm a person with a view. But I feel calm now, calmer than I would have if I had stayed and argued.

Thank you for always letting me say things half-formed.

Alka

qa.q: What labels did the relative use for Alka?
qa.a: The relative called Alka brainwashed and anti-national.

qa.q: How did Alka feel, and how did Alka handle it?
qa.a: Alka felt stung, with burning cheeks and an urge to fire back, but answered briefly and walked away to get tea.

qa.q: What could Alka do if the relative brings it up again?
qa.a: State the view briefly, decline to be defined by the label, and end the conversation calmly.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel on reading this letter?
qa.a: Trusted, since Alka thanks Jasleen for always letting half-formed thoughts be said.

grounding: Alka is dismissed as brainwashed and anti-national, states a view briefly, ends the talk calmly and refuses to be defined by the label.
